item.title: [The Lancet] [Editorial] Climate change and health: 10 years on, what next?
item.description: The Paris Agreement came into force in 2016, a watershed in collective international action on climate change. That year also saw the creation of the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change, established to track the health effects of climate change and climate action. The past 10 years may have brought disheartening setbacks in climate policy, but there have also been huge advances in the understanding of and attitudes towards climate change.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Beyond the models: addressing the catastrophic health threats facing humanity requires a holistic approach

item.title: [The Lancet] [Comment] Offline: China bids to lead in global health
item.description: China's last-minute nomination of Dr Song Li as a candidate for Director-General (DG) of WHO surprised many observers of global health politics. But from the perspective of an emerging superpower, it was not surprising at all. The Chinese Government is ready to assert its claim to positions of global leadership, especially now that the USA has turned its back on multilateralism. In Beijing last week, I sat down with Dr Li to listen to her set out her manifesto. She has four pillars supporting her pitch: a more efficient WHO; a safer world; equitable health systems; and harnessing innovation.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] Jemilah Mahmood: Malaysian leadership in planetary health
item.description: In 2000, Professor Jemilah Mahmood watched television images of devastating floods in Mozambique as a helicopter rescued a woman giving birth in a tree. As an obstetrician and gynaecologist, the image stayed with her for nearly two decades. In 2019, while visiting clinics established after the floods, a midwife pointed to a young adult and said, “Their mother gave birth in a tree in the last flood.” Mahmood recalls: “It really hit me…we’ve been putting band aids on gaping wounds all these years.” She continues: “We just respond and we react and we don’t look at the underlying drivers of why wo

item.title: [The Lancet] [Perspectives] High-risk pregnancy after Dobbs: who is allowed to choose?
item.description: David N Hackney opens his book Impossible Choices: A Physician's Guidance on High-Risk Pregnancy in a World Without Roe on June 24, 2022, with a description of how unprepared he and his colleagues were for the US Supreme Court's decision in Dobbs v Jackson Women's Health Organization (hereafter Dobbs) that eliminated the constitutional right to abortion. Within hours, a near-total abortion ban took effect in Ohio. item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] North Korea's health revolution in its 2026 medical journals
item.description: Although North Korea remains largely closed to the rest of the world, its recent state messaging suggests a shift in the country's approach to health care from long-standing isolation towards selective modernisation and digitalisation. Kim Jong Un's designation of 2025 as the first year of a health revolution warrants renewed attention to North Korean medical journals, which remain under-read in global health.1

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Global health: dying from failure or fulfilment?
item.description: Richard Horton asks whether global health can recover its lost radicalism, referring to Saul Alinsky's Reveille for Radicals.1 Alinsky's ideas also reached Japan, where the book was translated and published in 1972.2 This Japanese translation arrived at precisely a moment when questions of citizen participation, organisation, and power had unusual resonance in Japan amid growing citizen movements against industrial pollution and other social problems.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Women with obstetric fistula in Somalia deserve better
item.description: Obstetric fistula is a devastating morbidity that rightly merits investigation and advocacy, as attempted in the World Report by Clotilde Bigot.1 However, we are dismayed by the quality of this reporting, which did not fact check the claims of its single source. The report does not meet the rigorous editorial standards that we expect from The Lancet. It does a disservice to vulnerable women who have obstetric fistula in Somalia and beyond.

item.title: [The Lancet] [Correspondence] Women with obstetric fistula in Somalia deserve better – Author's reply
item.description: I would like to thank Carrie J Ngongo and colleagues for taking the time to write their Correspondence and for highlighting important aspects of obstetric fistula care in Somalia that could not be fully addressed within the constraints of the World Report.1
